nameStory: The Eastern Elliptio gets its name from its elliptical or oval-shaped shell, which looks like a flattened football when viewed from above. The scientific name 'complanata' means 'flattened,' perfectly describing this mussel's streamlined profile that helps it nestle into river and lake bottoms.
description: The Eastern Elliptio is a freshwater mussel that lives buried in the muddy or sandy bottoms of New England's rivers, ponds, and lakes. This oval-shaped bivalve has two hinged shells that protect its soft body inside, much like a clam but adapted for fresh water instead of the ocean. These mussels can grow up to 5 inches long, making them one of the larger freshwater shellfish you might encounter. They're incredibly common throughout New England waterways, often being the most abundant mussel species in their home streams and ponds.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly oval or elliptical shell that feels smooth and streamlined, like a flattened egg. The shell is noticeably longer than it is tall, giving it that characteristic football-like outline.

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish exterior that may feel slightly rough with growth rings, while the interior reveals a pearly white or bluish-white surface that's smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Can reach up to 5 inches in length, though most specimens you'll find are 2-4 inches long. Feels surprisingly heavy and solid when picked up.

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Exterior has concentric growth rings that you can feel with your finger, like tree rings, showing the mussel's age. The surface may have a slightly chalky or gritty texture.

idTips.label: Hinge Area
idTips.description: Strong hinge with visible teeth that lock the two shell halves together. When fresh, the shells clamp shut tightly and require significant force to open.

idTips.label: Location in Water
idTips.description: Found partially buried in soft sediment with only the back edge exposed for filter-feeding. Look for slight depressions or tracks in muddy lake or river bottoms.

habitat: Eastern Elliptios thrive in the soft, muddy or sandy bottoms of slow-moving rivers, streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England. They prefer areas with gentle currents where they can burrow partway into the sediment while still accessing the flowing water they need for feeding. You'll often find them in the shallower areas of larger water bodies, typically in depths ranging from a few inches to several feet deep.

seasonality.spring: As water temperatures warm, mussels become more active and may be easier to spot as they move through sediment. This is their reproductive season when they release larvae.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're actively filter-feeding. Look for feeding signs like small siphon holes in the sediment or slight water currents near buried mussels.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down. Empty shells from natural mortality become more noticeable on shorelines after storms wash them up.
seasonality.winter: Buried deep in sediment and largely inactive. Empty shells are most commonly found washed up on shores, especially after ice-out when spring flooding redistributes them.

funFact: Eastern Elliptios are living water purifiers that can filter up to 15 gallons of water per day through their bodies, removing bacteria, algae, and particles to help keep our waterways clean — making a single mussel bed like having a natural water treatment plant working 24/7 in your local stream!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other freshwater mussels, but the Eastern Elliptio's distinctly oval, elongated shape sets it apart from rounder species. Remember: 'Elliptio = Elliptical' — if the shell looks like a flattened oval rather than round or triangular, you've likely found an Eastern Elliptio.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'mussel,' freshwater mussels like the Eastern Elliptio are quite different from the marine mussels you might see at a seafood restaurant. Freshwater mussels have a completely different lifestyle, living buried in sediment rather than attached to rocks, and they play a crucial ecological role as natural water filters in our rivers and lakes.
compareHints: As the only Elliptio species commonly found in New England, the Eastern Elliptio is most similar to other river mussels in the Unionidae family. However, it stands out from its relatives with its distinctly elongated, oval shape — while other freshwater mussels tend to be more rounded, triangular, or fan-shaped. Its smooth, streamlined profile is quite different from the more angular or ribbed shells of other mussel species in the region.
